evidence_audit.text: Mixer speed and duration are set for each mixing operation.
Mechanical testing includes 24-hour and 28-day groups, with three prisms in each group.

This check covers only the 28-day group from the same mixing operation and the same curing regimen: the three prisms each undergo flexural testing, followed by compression testing of the two half-prisms produced from each prism.

The methods record curing environment category and temperature by batch.
In the water-curing branch, a water bath at a set temperature is used from demolding until day 28; an in-bath probe measures the water temperature.
Mechanical testing at 28 days uses a group of three prisms from that batch.
Figure 2 shows the curing equipment, including a photograph of a water bath.
Four copper strips enter a single treatment together.
Temperature and concentration apply jointly to this group; within the group, two strips are randomly assigned to low current and two to high current.
Each of the four temperature-concentration combinations is run once.

The source explicitly defines a single copper strip as the experimental unit for current (subplot experimental unit), and the group of four strips treated together as the unit for temperature and concentration (whole-plot experimental unit).

A continuous nickel-alloy combinatorial specimen contains multiple column regions, each processed at a specified laser power and scan speed.
Columns 1, 10, 16, 19, and 24 in Table 2 use the same default settings.
The study produced multiple specimens of the same geometry; one whole specimen received stress-relief treatment at 800°C and another at 870°C.
The authors explicitly describe a split-plot design because each combinatorial specimen was fabricated and stress-relieved as a continuous whole.
Multiple indentation measurements were then taken within each column region.
This check covers only the combinatorial specimen treated at 870°C and the default-setting columns listed above; other specimens and columns are excluded.

Wear scars are generated at different circumferential positions on a cutter.
Each scar results from a machining operation performed by one operator, who then scans that scar three times.
The first character of PART ID identifies the cutter, and the second identifies the wear scar.
From Figure 2.6, this check selects six scan records for cutter 1, PART IDs 1A and 1B: 1A, 1A, and 1A are assigned to operator O1; 1B, 1B, and 1B are assigned to operator O3; 1C and 1D are excluded.
